literal: yoking; (from yuj 'to concentrate', per Vyāsa and Bhoja) concentration

definitions.definition: The stilling of the activities of the mind (YS 1.2); Vyāsa: 'yoga is samādhi', a property of the mind at all its levels, counting as yoga only in the one-pointed and stilled mind.

literal: mind; that which is conscious (as if)

definitions.definition: The mind, a product of prakṛti made of the three guṇas, whose activities are to be stilled; it is seen, not self-luminous, and exists for the sake of the puruṣa; one, having many objects, and enduring (YBh 1.32). Commentators gloss it as the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa).

equivalents.note: Nāgeśa glosses citta as antaḥkaraṇa; Yoga uses citta for the whole inner organ (buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas together) rather than naming its parts.

definitions.definition: An activity (modification) of the mind; five kinds — valid cognition, error, conceptual construction, sleep and memory — each afflicted or unafflicted (YS 1.5–6); the seer, when not in its own form, conforms to them (1.4).

cross_language.note: rare in this sense in Pali

definitions.definition: The stilling of the mind's activities, achieved by practice and dispassion (1.2, 1.12); as a transformation it is the mind's being joined to the moment of stilling as impressions of stilling overpower those of emergence (3.9); Nāgeśa calls it a supersensible effort of restraint that dissolves the activities.

cross_language.note: in Buddhism the cessation of suffering / of perception and feeling; different doctrinal frame

definitions.definition: Said of activities caused by the afflictions that become the field for accumulating karmic residue (YBh 1.5).
Said of activities that have discernment as their object and oppose the operation of the guṇas (YBh 1.5).
The first activity of mind: valid cognition, of three kinds — perception, inference and testimony (YS 1.7).

Perception: the mind's activity, coloured by an external thing through the senses, that chiefly ascertains the particular; its result is the puruṣa's awareness of the activity (YBh 1.7). The perception of nirvitarkā samāpatti is the 'highest perception', the seed of testimony and inference (YBh 1.42).
Inference: an activity that chiefly ascertains the general through a relation present in like and absent from unlike cases (YBh 1.7); it reaches only the general (1.49, YBh 1.25).

literal: what has come down; testimony, scripture

definitions.definition: Testimony: the activity arising in a hearer from the words of a reliable speaker who has seen or inferred the matter (YBh 1.7); it too reaches only the general (1.49).
Error, false knowledge resting on a form not the object's own, sublated by valid cognition; as five-jointed ignorance it is the five afflictions (YS 1.8, YBh 1.8, 2.3).
An activity that follows on verbal knowledge but has no real object (1.9); in samāpatti, the mixing of word, object and cognition that marks savitarkā coalescence (1.42).
Sleep: the activity whose support is the cognition of absence (1.10); a cognition, since it is recollected on waking, and to be stilled in samādhi (YBh 1.10).

(1) Memory: the not-slipping-away of an experienced object (1.11); memory and impressions are of one form (4.9). (2) In YS 1.20, mindfulness, the third of the five means (faith, energy, mindfulness, samādhi, insight).

cross_language.note: as the faculty of 1.20; Buddhist mindfulness

notes: Homonym: the id trm:smrti is also used for 'remembered tradition'; this entry gives the Yoga senses.

definitions.definition: A latent impression left by activities, producing further activities in a ceaseless wheel (YBh 1.5); impressions of samādhi-insight obstruct others (1.50); impressions of stilling are a mental property (3.9); their direct perception gives knowledge of former births (3.18).

cross_language.note: Buddhist 'formations', a wider sense

definitions.definition: Latent tendencies from past experience that manifest only when suited to ripening karma (4.8), continuous across births (4.9), beginningless because the will to be is eternal (4.10), and ceasing when cause, result, substrate and support cease (4.11).
A cognition or presented content of the mind (1.10, 3.2, 3.19, 4.27); also 'cause' in upāya-/bhava-pratyaya (1.19–20).
The support or object on which the mind rests (1.10, 1.38); samādhis with a support are samprajñāta (YBh 1.17).
The seer's taking on the form of the mind's activities when not stilled (1.4).
The seer's abiding in its own form (1.3), and kaivalya as the power of consciousness established in its own form (4.34).
The seer, the puruṣa: seeing alone, pure, seeing by conforming to cognitions (2.20); the witness of the buddhi (YBh 2.17); its conjunction with the seen is the cause of suffering (2.17).
The seen: of the nature of illumination, activity and inertia, consisting of elements and senses, for experience and liberation (2.18), existing for the seer's sake (2.21).

literal: person; the self as pure consciousness

definitions.definition: The seer, pure consciousness, unchanging, not self-luminous objects' owner but always knowing the mind's activities (4.18); utterly unmixed with sattva (3.35); many (2.22).

equivalents.note: Yoga texts call the seer 'ātman' (2.5 'anātmany ātmakhyātiḥ', 2.41 'ātmadarśana'), but the Yoga puruṣa is plural and actionless, unlike the one ātman of Advaita.

definitions.definition: The puruṣa as the power of consciousness: unchanging, not passing over into objects, pure and infinite (YBh 1.2); kaivalya is its establishment in its own form (4.34).
Material nature, the seen, of three guṇas; in YS 4.2–3 'prakṛti' (plural) are the material causes whose overflow transforms beings.

equivalents.note: In the Yoga texts pradhāna names the unmanifest prakṛti (YBh 2.18–19, YS 3.48).

definitions.definition: The guṇas as the unmanifest source, 'neither being nor non-being' (YBh 2.19); mastery of pradhāna is one of the three 'honey-like' powers (3.48).

The three constituents of the seen — sattva (illumination), rajas (activity), tamas (inertia) (2.18); their conflicting activity makes all suffering for the discerning (2.15); everything is a particular arrangement of them (4.13); at kaivalya they return to their source (4.34).
The guṇa of illumination; in YS 3.35, 3.49, 3.55 the buddhi-sattva, whose purity equal to the puruṣa's is kaivalya, and whose difference from the puruṣa is discerned in viveka-khyāti.
The instrument of cognition (the 'power of seeing') whose apparent identity with the seer is I-am-ness (YBh 2.6); neither the same as the puruṣa nor wholly different (YBh 2.20).
Used in YS for the mind made fit for concentrations (2.53) and steadied (1.35); YBh 2.19 counts manas as the eleventh sense.
The senses (ten, with manas eleven, YBh 2.19), part of the seen (2.18); withdrawn in pratyāhāra (2.54) and mastered by saṃyama on their five forms (3.47).
The conjunction of seer and seen, cause of what is to be avoided (2.17), caused by ignorance (2.24), the cause of apprehending owner and owned (2.23); its absence is kaivalya (2.25).

Experience: a cognition that fails to distinguish sattva and puruṣa (3.35); determining the guṇas as desired or undesired without discrimination (YBh 2.18); one of the two purposes of the seen (2.18).
Liberation as the second purpose of the seen: determining the enjoyer's own nature (2.18, YBh 2.18).
The first level of the guṇas: the sixteen particularized products — five elements, ten senses and mind (2.19, YBh 2.19).
The second level: the five tanmātras and I-am-ness alone (2.19, YBh 2.19).
The third level: the great principle (mahat), pure being, from which the unparticularized evolve (YBh 2.19).
The fourth level: the unmanifest pradhāna, subtlest of objects, beyond which nothing is subtler (1.45, 2.19).
The change of a property-bearer's manifest property (e.g. emergence giving way to stilling; lump to pot) (3.13).
The passage of a property from future to present to past time-path (3.13, YBh 3.13).
Change in the strength or condition of a present property (e.g. impressions of stilling growing strong; a pot's newness turning to age) (3.13, YBh 3.13, 3.15).
Real change of form in the guṇas and their products (3.9–15, 4.14, 4.32–33).
The substrate that conforms to properties past, present and not yet determinable (3.14).
The three time-paths (past, present, future) in which properties stand; past and future exist in their own form because of this difference (4.12).
The smallest unit of time, the time in which a moving atom passes from one point to the next; only the moment is real (YBh 3.52).

cross_language.note: Buddhist momentariness doctrine differs

definitions.definition: Sequence: the unbroken flow of moments, apprehended at the end of a transformation (3.15, 3.52, 4.33).
The unchanging permanence of the puruṣa (YBh 4.33).
The permanence of the guṇas, whose nature is not destroyed as they transform (YBh 4.33).
Practice: effort toward the mind's stability (1.13), firmly grounded when long, uninterrupted and devoted (1.14); with dispassion the means of stilling (1.12).

Dispassion: the consciousness of mastery of one free of thirst for seen and scriptural objects (1.15); the higher is freedom from thirst for the guṇas (1.16); dispassion even toward the highest powers leads to kaivalya (3.50).

cross_language.note: Buddhist dispassion

definitions.definition: The defining mark of lower dispassion (1.15); in Vācaspati the fourth of four stages of dispassion.
Freedom from thirst for the guṇas themselves, from discernment of the puruṣa (1.16); only the clarity of knowledge; the means to asamprajñāta samādhi (YBh 1.16, 1.18).
The first of the five means (1.20): serenity of mind which, like a kind mother, protects the yogin (YBh 1.20).
(1) Energy, the second means (1.20); (2) the vigour gained by one established in celibacy (2.38).
Insight: the fifth means (1.20); truth-bearing in nirvicāra lucidity (1.48); sevenfold at the final stage (2.27); its light comes from mastery of saṃyama (3.5).
Ardor in practice, mild, middling or intense; for the intensely ardent samādhi is near (1.21–22).

cross_language.note: Buddhist 'spiritual urgency'

definitions.definition: Samādhi arising from means (faith etc.), that of yogins (1.20, YBh 1.19–20).
The state of the bodiless and those merged in prakṛti, which has becoming as its cause (1.19); Vijñānabhikṣu glosses bhava as birth.
Beings who experience a state like kaivalya without a body; Vyāsa calls them gods (YBh 1.19); Bhoja: those who rest content in bliss-samādhi (RM 1.17).
Those whose mind, with its task unfinished, is dissolved in prakṛti, experiencing a quasi-kaivalya until it returns (YBh 1.19); Bhoja: those who rest content in I-am-ness samādhi (RM 1.17).

A special puruṣa untouched by afflictions, karma, fruition and residues (1.24), in whom the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed (1.25), teacher of the ancients (1.26), designated by the praṇava (1.27); his lordship has no equal or superior (YBh 1.24).
Īśvara's definition: a puruṣa distinguished from others by never having been touched by bondage (1.24, YBh 1.24).

Devotion to Īśvara: a special bhakti by which Īśvara, won over, favours the yogin (YBh 1.23); offering all actions to the supreme teacher or renouncing their fruit (YBh 2.1, RM 2.1); a means to samādhi (1.23, 2.45), part of kriyā-yoga (2.1) and a niyama (2.32).
The designator of Īśvara (1.27), whose relation to him is fixed, not conventional (YBh 1.27); repeated with contemplation of its meaning (1.28).

equivalents.note: praṇava is the name of the syllable Oṃ

definitions.definition: Repetition of the praṇava together with contemplation of Īśvara, making the mind one-pointed (1.28, YBh 1.28); self-study includes repetition of purifying formulas (YBh 2.1).
Cultivation: of the meaning of the praṇava (1.28), of the four attitudes (1.33), of the opposites of harmful thoughts (2.33); Vyāsa: equanimity toward the wicked is not a cultivation (YBh 3.23).

Īśvara is the teacher (guru) even of the ancients, unlimited by time (1.26); devotion offers all actions to the supreme teacher (paramaguru, YBh 2.1); Vyāsa: in the stages of saṃyama 'yoga itself is the teacher' (YBh 3.6).
The nine obstacles, distractions of the mind (1.30), removed through devotion to Īśvara (1.29) and practice on a single principle (1.32).
The name of the nine obstacles (1.30); called impurities of yoga and adversaries of yoga (YBh 1.30).
Illness: imbalance of the bodily elements, fluids and organs (YBh 1.30).
Dullness: the mind's unfitness for work (YBh 1.30).
Doubt: a cognition touching both alternatives (YBh 1.30).
Carelessness: not cultivating the means of samādhi (YBh 1.30); Vyāsa warns that carelessness watches for an opening to revive the afflictions (YBh 3.51).
Laziness: inactivity from heaviness of body and mind (YBh 1.30).
Non-abstention: the mind's greed for contact with objects (YBh 1.30).
Erroneous vision: false knowledge (YBh 1.30).
Failure to attain a stage of samādhi (YBh 1.30).
The mind's not being established in a stage it has gained (YBh 1.30).

Pain, the first accompaniment of distraction, threefold — from oneself, other beings, the gods (1.31, YBh 1.31); for the discerning everything is suffering (2.15); future suffering is what is to be avoided (2.16).
Agitation of mind from thwarted desire (YBh 1.31).
What shakes the limbs, an accompaniment of distraction (YBh 1.31); steady posture prevents it (YBh 2.47).
Drawing in outer air and expelling inner air (YBh 1.31, 2.49); disturbed, they accompany distraction (1.31); the cutting off of their movement is prāṇāyāma (2.49).
Resting the mind on a single principle to counter the obstacles (1.32, YBh 1.32).
Friendliness cultivated toward the happy, one of the four attitudes that clarify the mind (1.33, YBh 1.33). Saṃyama on it yields its strength (3.23).

cross_language.note: one of the four brahmavihāras (immeasurables); in Buddhism radiated to all beings

definitions.definition: Compassion cultivated toward the suffering, one of the four attitudes that clarify the mind (1.33, YBh 1.33). Saṃyama on it yields its strength (3.23).

cross_language.note: one of the four brahmavihāras (immeasurables); in Buddhism radiated to all beings

definitions.definition: Gladness cultivated toward the virtuous, one of the four attitudes that clarify the mind (1.33, YBh 1.33). Saṃyama on it yields its strength (3.23).

cross_language.note: one of the four brahmavihāras (immeasurables); in Buddhism radiated to all beings

definitions.definition: Equanimity, disregard cultivated toward the non-virtuous, one of the four attitudes that clarify the mind (1.33, YBh 1.33). Vyāsa: equanimity toward the wicked is not a cultivation and yields no strength (YBh 3.23).

cross_language.note: one of the four brahmavihāras (immeasurables); in Buddhism radiated to all beings

definitions.definition: The clearing of the mind that results from the four attitudes; the clear mind becomes one-pointed (1.33, YBh 1.33).

cross_language.note: Buddhist 'serenity/confidence of mind'

definitions.definition: The sorrowless, luminous activity (1.36): awareness of the buddhi in the heart-lotus, shining like sun, moon and gems, and I-am-ness alone like a waveless ocean (YBh 1.36); its light is directed in 3.25.
Yoga itself (YBh 1.1); the eighth limb — meditation shining only as its object, as if empty of its own form (3.3); of two kinds, samprajñāta and asamprajñāta; with seed or seedless.
Samādhi accompanied by reasoning, reflection, bliss or I-am-ness (1.17), with a support (YBh 1.17).
The 'other' samādhi, preceded by practice of the cognition of cessation, with only impressions remaining (1.18); nothing is cognized in it (YBh 1.2); means: higher dispassion (YBh 1.18).
The four samāpattis, which have an external thing as seed, are samādhi with seed (1.46, YBh 1.46).
Samādhi when even the impression of truth-bearing insight is stilled (1.51); the three inner limbs are outer limbs relative to it (3.8).

The mind's taking on the form of what it rests on — grasper, grasping or grasped — like a flawless crystal (1.41); fourfold: savitarkā, nirvitarkā, savicārā, nirvicārā (1.42–44); also coalescence with the endless in posture (2.47).

cross_language.note: Buddhist 'meditative attainment' (the jhānas and formless attainments)

definitions.definition: The grasper, the puruṣa (as it appears to the mind), one of the three objects of coalescence (1.41, YBh 1.41).
The grasping instruments, the senses (1.41); the first of the five forms of the senses mastered by saṃyama (3.47).
Objects to be grasped — gross and subtle elements, the world (1.41, YBh 1.41).

(1) The mind's gross engagement with its support, the mark of the first samprajñāta samādhi (1.17, YBh 1.17). (2) A distinct sense in 2.33–34: harmful thoughts such as violence, to be countered by cultivating their opposites.

cross_language.note: first-jhāna factor 'applied thought'

notes: Homonym within the YS itself; do not merge the two senses.

definitions.definition: The mind's subtle engagement with its support (YBh 1.17); coalescence with subtle objects (1.44).

cross_language.note: first-jhāna factor 'sustained thought'

definitions.definition: Joy (hlāda), the third level of samprajñāta samādhi (1.17, YBh 1.17); Vijñānabhikṣu: a joy arising from preponderant sattva; Bhoja: bliss when the inner organ's sattva is cultivated.

(1) The affliction: the seeming identity of the power of the seer and the power of seeing (2.6). (2) The fourth level of samprajñāta samādhi, awareness of a single self (YBh 1.17). (3) 'Asmitā-mātra', the sixth unparticularized principle (YBh 2.19) and the source of created minds (4.4).

equivalents.note: YBh 2.19 names the sixth unparticularized principle asmitā-mātra where Sāṃkhya names ahaṃkāra; Bhoja (RM 1.17) insists asmitā and ahaṃkāra are not the same.

definitions.definition: Coalescence mixed with the constructions of word, object and cognition (1.42).
Coalescence in which, memory purified, the object alone shines as if empty of its own form (1.43); the highest perception, seed of testimony and inference (YBh 1.42).
Coalescence with subtle objects delimited by place, time and cause (1.44, YBh 1.44).
Coalescence with subtle objects free of such delimitation; its lucidity brings inner clarity (1.44, 1.47).
Inner clarity in the lucidity of nirvicārā coalescence (1.47): a clear light of insight grasping things as they are, without sequence (YBh 1.47).
The insight arising in that clarity, which bears only truth (1.48), has the particular as its object unlike testimony and inference (1.49), and whose impression obstructs others (1.50).
Austerity, self-study and devotion to Īśvara (2.1), for cultivating samādhi and thinning the afflictions (2.2); taught for the unconcentrated mind (YBh 2.1).
Austerity: bearing the pairs of opposites, with vows as suitable (YBh 2.32); to be practised without disturbing the mind's clarity (YBh 2.1); destroys impurity and perfects body and senses (2.43).
Repetition of purifying formulas such as the praṇava, or study of scriptures on liberation (YBh 2.1, 2.32); brings contact with the chosen deity (2.44).

The five afflictions — ignorance, I-am-ness, attachment, aversion, clinging to life (2.3) — the five errors (YBh 2.3), rooted in ignorance (2.4), root of the karmic residue (2.12); thinned by kriyā-yoga, abandoned by meditation and involution (2.2, 2.10–11), ceasing through the cloud of dharma (4.30).

cross_language.note: Buddhist defilements; lists differ

definitions.definition: Taking the impermanent, impure, painful and non-self as permanent, pure, pleasant and self (2.5); the field of the other afflictions (2.4) and the cause of the conjunction (2.24); not the absence of knowledge but a contrary cognition (YBh 2.5).
Attachment, which follows on pleasure (2.7).
Aversion, which follows on pain (2.8).
Clinging to life, flowing by its own momentum, present even in the wise (2.9); the wish 'may I not cease, may I be', a fear of death that shows former births (YBh 2.9).
A state of the afflictions (2.4): Existing in the mind as mere potency, like seeds (YBh 2.4).
A state of the afflictions (2.4): Weakened by cultivating the opposite (YBh 2.4); kriyā-yoga thins the afflictions (2.2).
A state of the afflictions (2.4): Appearing again and again in alternation, e.g. anger not active while attachment is (YBh 2.4).
A state of the afflictions (2.4): Operating on an object (YBh 2.4).

The fifth state of the afflictions, in one whose affliction-seeds are burnt by reflection, who is 'skilled' and in the last body (YBh 2.4); burnt-seed impressions give rise to no cognitions (4.28, YBh 4.28).
Return of an effect into its cause: the subtle afflictions are abandoned by it (2.10); kaivalya is the involution of the guṇas (4.34).

The residue of meritorious and demeritorious action, rooted in the afflictions, to be experienced in this or a future birth (2.12); ripening as birth, life-span and experience (2.13); normally 'of one life' (YBh 2.13).
The fruition of karma: birth, life-span and experience (2.13), bearing joy or anguish (2.14).

literal: to be experienced in the seen (present) birth

definitions.definition: Karma ripening in this life, e.g. from intense practice or grave harm (2.12, YBh 2.12).

literal: to be experienced in an unseen birth

definitions.definition: Karma ripening in a future life; none remains for one whose afflictions are exhausted (YBh 2.12).
The karma of the yogin (4.7): not white, since he renounces the fruit; not black, since he does not take it up (YBh 4.7); others' karma is black, white-and-black, or white.
Life-span karma that ripens quickly, like a wet cloth spread out (3.22, YBh 3.22).
Life-span karma that ripens slowly, like a rolled-up wet cloth (3.22, YBh 3.22).
Signs of approaching death, personal, from other beings, or from the gods (YBh 3.22).
The self-wish 'may I not cease, may I be', eternal, which makes the latent tendencies beginningless (4.10, YBh 2.9, 4.10).
The mind born of meditation, which lays down no karmic residue (4.6, YBh 4.6).
One of the four parts of the śāstra, modelled on medicine (YBh 2.15): Suffering yet to come (2.16); saṃsāra full of suffering (YBh 2.15).

literal: cause of what is to be avoided

definitions.definition: One of the four parts of the śāstra, modelled on medicine (YBh 2.15): The conjunction of seer and seen (2.17).
One of the four parts of the śāstra, modelled on medicine (YBh 2.15): The absence of the conjunction, the seer's kaivalya (2.25).
One of the four parts of the śāstra, modelled on medicine (YBh 2.15): Unwavering discriminative discernment (2.26); right seeing (YBh 2.15).

The cognition of the difference between sattva and puruṣa (YBh 2.26); unwavering, it is the means of avoidance (2.26); the light of knowledge grows up to it (2.28); complete, it yields the cloud of dharma (4.29).
The sevenfold insight of the discerning yogin: four releases regarding what is to be done and three releases of the mind (2.27, YBh 2.27).
The meditation called the cloud of dharma (YBh 1.2); its fire burns the seeds of affliction (YBh 2.2); one who takes no interest even in it attains the cloud of dharma (4.29).
Taking no interest (seeking no gain) even in the highest reflection (4.29, YBh 4.29).
The samādhi of one who, detached even from the highest reflection, has complete discriminative discernment and no other cognitions (4.29, YBh 4.29); from it afflictions and karma cease (4.30).

notes: The same compound names the tenth bodhisattva ground (dharmameghā bhūmi) in Mahāyāna; see brw:mahayana-yoga-dharmamegha.

definitions.definition: The aloneness of the seer: the absence of the conjunction (2.25); arising when sattva and puruṣa are equal in purity (3.55) or from dispassion even toward the highest power (3.50); defined as the guṇas' return to their source, or the power of consciousness established in its own form (4.34).

cross_language.note: Jain kevala-jñāna, omniscient knowledge of the liberated soul — a different doctrine

equivalents.note: Kaivalya is Yoga's name for liberation; YBh 2.15 calls the goal 'mokṣa' and 2.26 calls discernment 'the path of mokṣa'. Yoga's liberation is isolation of one puruṣa, not union.

definitions.definition: The eight limbs: restraints, observances, posture, breath-regulation, sense-withdrawal, concentration, meditation, samādhi (2.29), whose practice destroys impurity (2.28).
The five restraints: non-harming, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, non-possessiveness (2.30); universal, the great vow (2.31).
The five observances: purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, devotion to Īśvara (2.32).
Not injuring any being in any way at any time; the root of the other restraints and observances (YBh 2.30); when established, hostility is abandoned in one's presence (2.35).

cross_language.note: first Jain vow

definitions.definition: Speech and mind according to fact, spoken for the good of all beings; truth that harms is a semblance of merit (YBh 2.30); when established, actions and fruits rest on one's word (2.36).
Freedom from desire for what is not one's own (YBh 2.30); when established, all jewels present themselves (2.37).
Restraint of the generative organ with the senses guarded (YBh 2.30); when established, vigour is gained (2.38).
Not appropriating objects, seeing the faults of acquiring, keeping, losing, attachment and harm (YBh 2.30); when steady, knowledge of the how of births (2.39).

cross_language.note: fifth Jain vow

definitions.definition: The restraints when unlimited by class, place, time or occasion (2.31, YBh 2.31).

cross_language.note: the Jain five great vows of the ascetic — a related but distinct list

definitions.definition: Outer purity (earth, water, pure food) and inner washing away of the mind's stains (YBh 2.32); yields disgust for one's body and non-contact with others, and purity of sattva up to fitness for seeing the self (2.40–41).
Not wanting more than the means at hand (YBh 2.32); yields unsurpassed happiness (2.42).
Countering harmful thoughts by reflecting on their endless fruit of suffering and ignorance (2.33–34).
The deity with whom self-study brings contact (2.44); Vyāsa: gods, sages and perfected beings appear to the one devoted to self-study (YBh 2.44).
Posture, steady and comfortable (2.46), achieved by relaxing effort and coalescence with the endless (2.47); Vyāsa lists seated postures such as padmāsana, bhadrāsana and svastika (YBh 2.46).
Pairs such as cold and heat, which no longer assail one who has mastered posture (2.48); bearing them is austerity (YBh 2.32).

The cutting off of the movement of inhalation and exhalation (2.49); external, internal or suspended, regulated by place, time and number (2.50); a fourth transcends both spheres (2.51); it thins the covering of the light (2.52).
The karma that covers discriminative knowledge, dwindling through prāṇāyāma (2.52) and destroyed by the great bodiless concentration (3.43).
Sense-withdrawal: the senses, disjoined from their objects, imitating the mind's own form (2.54), bringing supreme mastery of the senses (2.55).
Concentration: binding the mind to a place (3.1) — navel, heart-lotus, light in the head, tip of the nose or tongue, or an external object (YBh 3.1).
Meditation: the continuous flow of a single cognition on the place of concentration (3.2); the means of abandoning the afflictions' activities (2.11).

cross_language.note: Buddhist absorption levels — broader and differently structured

definitions.definition: Concentration, meditation and samādhi together on one object (3.4), the 'technical term' of the śāstra (YBh 3.4); its mastery gives the light of insight (3.5) and the powers.
Concentration, meditation and samādhi, inner relative to the first five limbs (3.7).
The first five limbs; even the inner three are outer relative to seedless samādhi (3.8).
The mind's outgoing, non-concentrated state, whose impressions are overpowered in stilling (3.9); powers count as powers only in it (3.37); kriyā-yoga is for the emergent (vyutthita) mind (YBh 2.1).
The mind's being joined to the moment of stilling as impressions of emergence are overpowered and those of stilling appear (3.9); its peaceful flow comes from impressions (3.10).
The dwindling of the mind's all-objectness and the rise of one-pointedness (3.11).
The state in which the subsiding and arising cognitions are alike (3.12).
One-pointedness of mind, a mental property that rises as all-objectness dwindles (3.11–12); a fruit of purity (2.41).

cross_language.note: a jhāna factor

definitions.definition: The mind's peaceful flow from the impressions of stilling (3.10, YBh 3.10).
The five levels of the mind — scattered, stupefied, distracted, one-pointed, stilled (YBh 1.1).
The scattered mind, the first level (YBh 1.1).
The stupefied mind, the second level (YBh 1.1).
The distracted mind; samādhi in it, subordinate to distraction, is not yoga (YBh 1.1).
The one-pointed mind, in which samprajñāta yoga occurs (YBh 1.1).
The stilled mind, in which asamprajñāta samādhi occurs (YBh 1.1).
The powers treated in the third pāda (Vibhūti-pāda) that arise from saṃyama.
Powers arising from birth, herbs, mantras, austerity or samādhi (4.1); those from samādhi are obstacles in samādhi but powers in emergence (3.37).
What the powers are within samādhi, because they oppose seeing (3.37, YBh 3.37).
Intuition, forerunner of knowledge born of discrimination, like dawn before sunrise (3.33, YBh 3.33); with divine hearing, touch, sight, taste and smell arising from knowledge of the puruṣa (3.36).
The navel wheel, locus of concentration (YBh 3.1) and of saṃyama giving knowledge of the body's arrangement (3.29).
The pit of the throat below the tongue and throat; saṃyama there stops hunger and thirst (3.30, YBh 3.30).
A tortoise-shaped channel in the chest below the throat-well; saṃyama there gives steadiness (3.31, YBh 3.31).
A luminous opening inside the skull; saṃyama there gives sight of the perfected beings (3.32, YBh 3.32).
The breath expelled and retained in 1.34; the chief of the five vital airs, moving through mouth and nose up to the heart (YBh 3.39).
The vital air that leads upward, operating up to the head; its mastery gives non-adherence to water, mud and thorns and departure at death at will (3.39, YBh 3.39).
The vital air that distributes evenly, operating up to the navel; its mastery gives radiance (3.40, YBh 3.39–40).
Departure from the body at death, undertaken at will by one who has mastered udāna (3.39, YBh 3.39).
The mind's entering another body after loosening the cause of bondage and knowing its pathways (3.38); the senses follow it like bees their queen (YBh 3.38).
An unimagined activity of mind outside the body, which destroys the covering of the light (3.43).
From saṃyama on the five forms of the elements (3.44).
Supreme mastery of the senses from sense-withdrawal (2.55); also from saṃyama on their five forms (3.47); Vyāsa records several views of what it is (YBh 2.55).

The eight lordly powers — minuteness, lightness, greatness, reach, irresistible will, control, lordship, and settling things at will (YBh 3.45); Īśvara's lordship, which has no equal or superior (YBh 1.24).
Beauty, grace, strength and adamantine firmness (3.46).
Name of the three powers of 3.48 — swiftness like mind, action without instruments, mastery of pradhāna (YBh 3.48).
Knowledge from saṃyama on the moment and its sequence (3.52), discerning even indistinguishable things (3.53); the deliverer, all-embracing and without sequence (3.54).
Knowledge born of discrimination as arising from one's own intuition, not from instruction (3.54, YBh 3.54); also a name of intuition (YBh 3.33).
Minds created from I-am-ness alone (4.4), directed by one mind (4.5); only the meditation-born is without residue (4.6); the first knower taught Āsuri through a created mind (YBh 1.25).
One of Vyāsa's four kinds of yogin (YBh 3.51): The beginner, in whom the light has only begun to shine.
One of Vyāsa's four kinds of yogin (YBh 3.51): One at the honey stage, whose insight is truth-bearing; the celestials invite him (YBh 3.51).
One of Vyāsa's four kinds of yogin (YBh 3.51): One who has mastered the elements and senses and guards what has been cultivated.

literal: one who has passed beyond what is to be cultivated

definitions.definition: One of Vyāsa's four kinds of yogin (YBh 3.51): One whose sole aim is the dissolution of the mind, with the sevenfold final insight.
The stage at which the celestials invite the yogin (YBh 3.51); 'the lamp of yoga' from this stage on is part of knowledge born of discrimination (YBh 3.54).
